claim: Mammalian spindles are built from microtubule bundles called kinetochore-fibers (k-fibers) that attach to chromosomes and focus into spindle poles.
source: Mammalian spindles are built from a network of microtubules, including discrete bundles of microtubules connecting chromosomes to poles. These bundles, called kinetochore-fibers (k-fibers), are made of many microtubules, some of which directly extend from kinetochores to poles (Kiewisz et al., 2022; McDonald et al., 1992; O'Toole et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work (Kiewisz et al., 2022; McDonald et al., 1992; O'Toole et al., 2020) describing k-fiber structure.

claim: Dynein and other motors work together to focus microtubules into asters and poles in many systems.
source: In many systems, dynein and other motors work together to focus microtubules into asters and poles (Compton, 1998; Goshima et al., 2005a; Heald et al., 1996; Merdes et al., 1996; Roostalu et al., 2018; So et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to prior studies (Compton, 1998; Goshima et al., 2005a; Heald et al., 1996; Merdes et al., 1996; Roostalu et al., 2018; So et al., 2022).

claim: K-fiber microtubules turn over on the order of minutes in mammals.
source: In mammals, k-fiber microtubules turn over on the order of minutes (Gorbsky and Borisy, 1989), detaching from kinetochores and getting replaced.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Gorbsky and Borisy, 1989.

claim: K-fiber microtubules exhibit poleward flux, where k-fiber tubulin moves toward poles, with k-fiber plus-ends on average polymerizing and minus-ends appearing to depolymerize at poles.
source: They also exhibit poleward flux, where k-fiber tubulin moves toward poles, with k-fiber plus-ends on average polymerizing and minus-ends appearing to depolymerize at poles (Mitchison, 1989).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Mitchison, 1989.

claim: Biochemical factors and mechanical force are thought to tune k-fiber dynamics at both microtubule ends and thereby tune k-fiber length.
source: Both biochemical factors (Goshima and Scholey, 2010) and mechanical force (Akiyoshi et al., 2010; Dumont and Mitchison, 2009b; Nicklas and Staehly, 1967) are thought to tune k-fiber dynamics at both microtubule ends and thereby tune k-fiber length.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work on biochemical factors (Goshima and Scholey, 2010) and mechanical force (Akiyoshi et al., 2010; Dumont and Mitchison, 2009b; Nicklas and Staehly, 1967).

claim: Some spindles, such as in land plants, do not have focused poles.
source: Some spindles, such as in land plants, do not have focused poles (Yamada and Goshima, 2017), and in many species, spindles are composed of short, tiled microtubules indirectly connecting chromosomes to poles (Brugués et al., 2012; Yang et al., 2007), unlike mammalian k-fibers.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Yamada and Goshima, 2017.

claim: Overexpression of the dynactin subunit p50 (dynamitin) dissociates the dynactin complex and inhibits the pole-focusing forces of dynein.
source: p50 overexpression dissociates the dynactin complex and inhibits the pole-focusing forces of its binding partner, dynein (Echeverri et al., 1996; Howell et al., 2001; Quintyne et al., 1999), unfocusing poles in species such as Xenopus and Drosophila (Gaetz and Kapoor, 2004; Sharp et al., 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work (Echeverri et al., 1996; Howell et al., 2001; Quintyne et al., 1999; Gaetz and Kapoor, 2004; Sharp et al., 2000).

claim: Unfocused spindles correlated with higher mean intensity levels of p50 expression.
source: Indeed, we found that unfocused spindles correlated with higher mean intensity levels of p50 expression (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), consistent with prior work showing mild pole disruption vs. severe unfocusing depending on the severity of dynein inhibition (Elting et al., 2017; Gaglio et al., 1997, p. 199; Hueschen et al., 2019; Hueschen et al., 2017; Sharp et al., 2000, p. 200; van Toorn et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and citations to prior work (Elting et al., 2017; Gaglio et al., 1997, p. 199; Hueschen et al., 2019; Hueschen et al., 2017; Sharp et al., 2000, p. 200; van Toorn et al., 2022).

claim: K-fibers in p50-overexpressing cells eventually lost their connection to centrosomes and became unfocused.
source: While k-fibers seemed initially focused in these cells, these k-fibers eventually lost their connection to centrosomes and became unfocused, exhibiting a similar phenotype to spindle assembly in some NuMA-disrupted cells (Figure 1A, Figure 1—videos 1 and 2, Silk et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by observations shown in Figure 1A and Figure 1—videos 1 and 2, and a citation to Silk et al., 2009.

claim: Disconnected centrosomes seemingly move around freely in cells with unfocused spindles.
source: We observed disconnected centrosomes seemingly move around freely in cells with unfocused spindles (Figure 1—videos 2 and 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by observations shown in Figure 1—videos 2 and 3.

claim: Unfocused metaphase spindles were barrel-shaped with bi-oriented chromosomes and underwent anaphase after several hours instead of about 30 min in control.
source: The resulting metaphase spindles were barrel-shaped with bi-oriented chromosomes, and they underwent anaphase after several hours instead of about 30 min in control, consistent with dynein inhibition at kinetochores causing an anaphase delay (Howell et al., 2001; Figure 1A, Figure 1—videos 1 and 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by observations shown in Figure 1A and Figure 1—videos 1 and 2, and a citation to Howell et al., 2001.

claim: The interkinetochore distance in unfocused spindles was indistinguishable from control.
source: Their interkinetochore distance was indistinguishable from control (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), suggesting that k-fibers are still under some tension from other forces (Elting et al., 2017; Kajtez et al., 2016; Maiato et al., 2004; Milas and Tolić, 2016), despite not being connected to poles.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2 and citations to prior work (Elting et al., 2017; Kajtez et al., 2016; Maiato et al., 2004; Milas and Tolić, 2016).

claim: p50 overexpression in human RPE1 cells led to similar unfocusing phenotypes as in PtK2 cells.
source: p50 overexpression in human RPE1 cells led to similar unfocusing phenotypes (Figure 1—figure supplement 3), but k-fibers were not individually resolvable.
evidence: The claim is supported by observations shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: Unfocused spindles had k-fibers that were more spread out in the cell, with spindles covering a larger area compared to control along both its major and minor axes.
source: We first observed that in unfocused spindles, k-fibers were more spread out in the cell, with spindles covering a larger area compared to control along both its major and minor axes (Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 4A).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 4A.

claim: Mean k-fiber length in an unfocused spindle (7.81 ± 2.52 µm) was not significantly different than control (8.01 ± 1.76 µm).
source: Mean k-fiber length in an unfocused spindle (7.81 ± 2.52 µm) was not significantly different than control (8.01 ± 1.76 µm) (Figure 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative measurements shown in Figure 1E.

claim: K-fibers do not require a pole connection to keep their mean length.
source: Thus, k-fibers do not require a pole connection to keep their mean length.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that mean k-fiber length is indistinguishable between control and unfocused spindles.

claim: Unfocused spindles showed a greater standard deviation in k-fiber lengths compared to control.
source: However, these unfocused spindles showed a greater standard deviation in lengths, so we compared average k-fiber lengths per cell to account for cell-to-cell variability: the mean k-fiber length within each cell was indistinguishable between control and unfocused cells (Figure 1F), but the standard deviation was significantly greater in unfocused cells (Figure 1G).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1F and Figure 1G.

claim: Spindle poles act to synchronize lengths between neighbors within a spindle, rather than to set and keep length.
source: This indicates that spindle poles act to synchronize lengths between neighbors within a spindle, rather than to set and keep length.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that mean k-fiber length is similar but standard deviation is greater in unfocused spindles.

claim: Unfocused k-fibers have indistinguishable mean lengths averaged over time compared to control but a greater coefficient of variation in lengths over time.
source: We observed indistinguishable mean lengths averaged over time in unfocused and control k-fibers and a greater coefficient of variation in unfocused k-fiber lengths over time compared to control (Figure 1I, J).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1I and Figure 1J.

claim: Outer k-fibers are longer than inner k-fibers in control spindles, but this difference was lost in unfocused spindles.
source: Based on geometry and previous observations, we expected outer k-fibers to be longer than inner k-fibers in focused spindles (Kiewisz et al., 2022). This was indeed the case in control spindles, but this difference was lost in unfocused spindles (Figure 1—figure supplement 6A).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 6A and a citation to Kiewisz et al., 2022.

claim: K-fiber length correlates with distance to the metaphase plate in control spindles but not in unfocused spindles.
source: Furthermore, we expected k-fiber length to correlate with distance to the metaphase plate – k-fibers are shorter if attached to under-aligned chromosomes and longer if attached to over-aligned chromosomes (Wan et al., 2012). Here too, a correlation between k-fiber length and alignment was observed in control but it was negligible in unfocused spindles (Figure 1—figure supplement 6B).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 6B and a citation to Wan et al., 2012.

claim: In control cells, as one sister k-fiber shortened, the other elongated to maintain a constant sum of their lengths, but this was not observed in unfocused spindles.
source: During chromosome oscillations, sister k-fiber lengths are normally anti-correlated (Wan et al., 2012). Indeed, in control cells we observed that as one sister k-fiber shortened, the other elongated to maintain a constant sum of their lengths. However, this was not observed in unfocused spindles (Figure 1K).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1K and a citation to Wan et al., 2012.

claim: The sum of sister k-fiber lengths was indistinguishable from control when averaged over time, but their sum was less conserved over time in unfocused spindles, yielding higher coefficients of variation.
source: In unfocused spindles, the sum of sister k-fiber lengths was indistinguishable from control when averaged over time, but their sum was less conserved over time, yielding higher coefficients of variation (Figure 1K–N).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1K–N.

claim: Spindle poles are not required to globally maintain k-fiber length.
source: Together, our findings indicate that spindle poles are not required to globally maintain k-fiber length.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that mean k-fiber length is maintained in unfocused spindles.

claim: Individual k-fibers can locally maintain their length scale over time, and poles and global pole-focusing forces are needed to coordinate k-fiber lengths within the cell and across sister k-fibers.
source: Instead, individual k-fibers can locally maintain their length scale over time, and poles and global pole-focusing forces are needed to coordinate k-fiber lengths within the cell and across sister k-fibers, organizing the spindle's structure in space and time.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the combined observations that mean k-fiber length is maintained but coordination is lost in unfocused spindles.

claim: Control ablated k-fibers were transported toward poles and grew back rapidly following ablation, at 0.85 ± 0.09 µm/min on average in the first 5 min.
source: As expected, control ablated k-fibers were transported toward poles and did so while growing back rapidly following ablation, at 0.85 ± 0.09 µm/min on average in the first 5 min (Figure 2E).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative measurements shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Unfocused k-fibers grew back after ablation, though more slowly at 0.38 ± 0.42 µm/min on average.
source: Unfocused k-fibers also grew back, though more slowly at 0.38 ± 0.42 µm/min on average (Figure 2E).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative measurements shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Focused poles and pole-focusing forces are not required for k-fibers to recover their lengths, but are required for rapid length recovery.
source: Thus, focused poles and pole-focusing forces are not required for k-fibers to recover their lengths, but are required for rapid length recovery.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that unfocused k-fibers can regrow but do so more slowly than control.

claim: After 10 min of nocodazole washout, control spindle k-fibers had regrown to within 1 µm of their original length, albeit shorter on average, and unfocused spindle k-fibers fully recovered their average length.
source: After 10 min, control spindle k-fibers had regrown to within 1 µm of their original length, albeit shorter on average, and unfocused spindle k-fibers fully recovered their average length and grew back into an unfocused state (Figure 2G–I, Figure 2—video 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2G–I and Figure 2—video 2.

claim: Both control and unfocused spindles could enter anaphase after nocodazole washout.
source: Both control and unfocused spindles could enter anaphase after nocodazole washout (Figure 2G, Figure 2—video 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by observations shown in Figure 2G and Figure 2—video 2.

claim: Cells lacking pole-focusing forces in metaphase can self-assemble unfocused spindles with k-fibers of about the same length as control k-fibers.
source: Thus, cells lacking pole-focusing forces in metaphase can self-assemble unfocused spindles with k-fibers of about the same length as control k-fibers.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that unfocused spindles can reassemble after nocodazole washout with similar k-fiber lengths.

claim: Unfocused k-fibers have stronger autocorrelation and autocorrelation for a longer period compared to control, consistent with reduced dynamics.
source: If k-fibers were less dynamic and their lengths changed more slowly, this would result in stronger autocorrelation and autocorrelation for a longer period. Indeed, this is what we observed in unfocused k-fibers compared to control, consistent with unfocused k-fibers having reduced dynamics (Figure 3A).
evidence: The claim is supported by autocorrelation analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: In control spindles, the photomark approached minus-ends at a rate of 0.55 ± 0.29 µm/min.
source: In control spindles, the mark approached minus-ends at a rate of 0.55 ± 0.29 µm/min, consistent with previous reports (Figures 3D and 4D, Cameron et al., 2006; Mitchison, 1989).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative measurements shown in Figures 3D and 4D, and citations to Cameron et al., 2006 and Mitchison, 1989.

claim: In unfocused spindles, the photomark approached minus-ends much slower at a rate of 0.13±0.15 µm/min.
source: In unfocused spindles, the mark approached minus-ends much slower at a rate of 0.13±0.15 µm/min (Figures 3D and 4D).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative measurements shown in Figures 3D and 4D.

claim: Spindle poles or pole-focusing forces are required for fast k-fiber end dynamics.
source: Thus, spindle poles or pole-focusing forces are required for fast k-fiber end dynamics, likely contributing to less efficient k-fiber length maintenance in unfocused spindles.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that unfocused k-fibers have slower flux rates.

claim: K-fibers can grow back after ablation at a rate faster than poleward flux in both control and unfocused spindles.
source: Notably, we find that k-fibers can grow back after ablation (Figure 2E) at a rate faster than poleward flux and associated minus-end dynamics in both control and unfocused spindles (0.85 ± 0.09 vs. 0.55 ± 0.29 µm/min in control, 0.38 ± 0.42 vs. 0.13 ± 0.15 µm/min in unfocused) (Figures 2E and 4D).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative measurements shown in Figures 2E and 4D.

claim: In control spindles, the photomark did not detectably approach the minus-end of the k-fiber during its regrowth after ablation.
source: In control spindles, the photomark did not detectably approach the minus-end of the k-fiber during its regrowth (Figure 4B, C), indicating that suppression of minus-end dynamics contributes to k-fiber regrowth, as in Drosophila cells (Maiato et al., 2004; Matos et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4B and C, and citations to Maiato et al., 2004 and Matos et al., 2009.

claim: K-fiber minus-ends resumed depolymerization in control spindles after ablation and length recovery.
source: Consistent with k-fiber minus-end dynamics being transiently suppressed during regrowth, rather than frozen due to ablation damage, k-fiber minus-ends resumed depolymerization in control spindles after ablation and length recovery (Figure 4—figure supplement 1, Figure 4—video 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1 and Figure 4—video 2.

claim: Mammalian k-fibers must additionally increase their plus-end dynamics when shortened to reestablish their steady-state length.
source: However, while Drosophila k-fibers regrow at the rate of poleward flux, these control mammalian k-fibers regrew faster than the rate of flux, indicating that mammalian k-fibers must additionally increase their plus-end dynamics when shortened to reestablish their steady-state length.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that k-fibers regrow faster than the flux rate.

claim: In unfocused spindles, the photomark did not detectably approach the minus-end of the k-fiber during its regrowth after ablation.
source: In unfocused spindles, the photomark also did not detectably approach the minus-end of the k-fiber during its regrowth (Figure 4C), consistent with suppression of any minus-end dynamics, though it was not significantly different from the already slow dynamics and insufficient to account for growth (Figure 4D).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4C and Figure 4D.

claim: K-fibers can tune their plus-end dynamics to recover their length in the absence of dynein-based pole-focusing forces.
source: Thus, k-fibers can tune their plus-end dynamics to recover their length in the absence of dynein-based pole-focusing forces.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that unfocused k-fibers can regrow after ablation despite suppressed minus-end dynamics.

claim: K-fiber length is not simply regulated by global pole-focusing forces, but by local length-based mechanisms.
source: This supports a model where k-fiber length is not simply regulated by global pole-focusing forces, but by local length-based mechanisms.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that k-fibers can tune their dynamics to recover length without pole-focusing forces.

claim: In spindles without focused poles, chromatids separated at twofold reduced velocities compared to control.
source: In spindles without focused poles, chromatids separated—albeit at twofold reduced velocities compared to control—in the separating chromatid pairs that could be identified (Figure 5C).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative measurements shown in Figure 5C.

claim: In the absence of poles or dynein activity, chromatid separation likely comes from pushing from the spindle center rather than from pulling from the cell cortex.
source: In the absence of poles or dynein activity, such chromatid separation likely comes from pushing from the spindle center rather than from pulling from the cell cortex (Vukušić et al., 2017; Yu et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Vukušić et al., 2017 and Yu et al., 2019.

claim: Major segregation and cytokinetic defects were observed in unfocused spindles compared to control.
source: However, major segregation and cytokinetic defects were observed in these cells compared to control, consistent with segregation defects observed in k-fibers disconnected from poles (van Toorn et al., 2022; Sivaram et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by observations and citations to van Toorn et al., 2022 and Sivaram et al., 2009.

claim: Cytokinetic defects and the presence of multiple cytokinetic furrows frequently resulted in the formation of more than two daughter cells in unfocused spindles.
source: Cytokinetic defects and the presence of multiple cytokinetic furrows frequently resulted in the formation of more than two daughter cells in unfocused spindles (Figure 5D).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Chromosome masses were scattered and unequally distributed in unfocused spindles, whereby control daughter cells inherited approximately half of the chromosome mass but not daughter cells of unfocused spindles.
source: Furthermore, chromosome masses were scattered and unequally distributed in these cells, whereby control daughter cells inherited approximately half of the chromosome mass as measured by DNA intensity, but not daughter cells of unfocused spindles (Figure 5E).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative measurements shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Spindle poles are essential to coordinate chromosome segregation and cytokinesis in mammalian cells.
source: Thus, while many species lack spindle poles, and while unfocused mammalian spindles can still maintain k-fiber length and separate chromatids, spindle poles are essential to coordinate chromosome segregation and cytokinesis in mammalian cells.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that unfocused spindles have severe segregation and cytokinesis defects.

claim: In the mammalian spindle, individual k-fibers set and maintain their lengths locally but require the global cue of a focused pole to coordinate their lengths across space and time.
source: Here, we show that in the mammalian spindle, individual k-fibers set and maintain their lengths locally but require the global cue of a focused pole to coordinate their lengths across space and time (Figure 6).
evidence: The claim summarizes the main findings of the study, supported by data throughout the manuscript and illustrated in Figure 6.

claim: Pole-less spindles can set and maintain k-fibers at the same mean length as in control, recovering their steady-state lengths if acutely shortened, but they have impaired dynamics and coordination and are unable to properly segregate chromosomes.
source: Our work reveals that pole-less spindles can set and maintain k-fibers at the same mean length as in control, recovering their steady-state lengths if acutely shortened, but they have impaired dynamics and coordination and are unable to properly segregate chromosomes.
evidence: The claim summarizes the main findings of the study.

claim: Length is an emergent property of individual k-fibers in the spindle, and spindle poles ensure that this network of k-fibers is highly dynamic and coordinated across space and time to ultimately cluster chromatids into two future daughter cells.
source: We propose a model whereby length is an emergent property of individual k-fibers in the spindle, and where spindle poles ensure that this network of k-fibers is highly dynamic and coordinated across space and time to ultimately cluster chromatids into two future daughter cells.
evidence: The claim is a proposed model based on the findings of the study.

claim: Spindle length scales with cell size during development.
source: The length of the spindle dictates the distance over which chromosomes segregate in dividing cells, and spindle length is known to scale with cell size during development (Good et al., 2013; Hazel et al., 2013; Lacroix et al., 2018; Rieckhoff et al., 2020; Wühr et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work (Good et al., 2013; Hazel et al., 2013; Lacroix et al., 2018; Rieckhoff et al., 2020; Wühr et al., 2008).

claim: Defects in spindle length are linked to impaired chromosome segregation, cytokinesis errors, and asymmetric division defects.
source: Defects in spindle length are linked to impaired chromosome segregation (Goshima et al., 1999), cytokinesis errors (Dechant and Glotzer, 2003), and asymmetric division defects (Dudka et al., 2019; Dumont et al., 2007), and long spindles have been hypothesized to come at an energetic cost (Dumont and Mitchison, 2009a).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work (Goshima et al., 1999; Dechant and Glotzer, 2003; Dudka et al., 2019; Dumont et al., 2007; Dumont and Mitchison, 2009a).

claim: Microtubule dynamics regulators with length-dependent activities could in principle give rise to the k-fiber's length scale.
source: Microtubule dynamics regulators with length-dependent activities (Dudka et al., 2019; Mayr et al., 2007; Stumpff et al., 2008; Varga et al., 2006) could in principle give rise to the k-fiber's length scale, beyond simply tuning length.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work (Dudka et al., 2019; Mayr et al., 2007; Stumpff et al., 2008; Varga et al., 2006).

claim: Global forces such as cell confinement pulls on poles, leading to k-fiber elongation by transiently suppressing apparent minus-end depolymerization.
source: For example, global forces such as cell confinement pulls on poles, leading to k-fiber elongation by transiently suppressing apparent minus-end depolymerization (Dumont and Mitchison, 2009b), but pole-less k-fibers do not elongate under these forces (Guild et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Dumont and Mitchison, 2009b and Guild et al., 2017.

claim: Locally pulling on a k-fiber with a microneedle causes it to stop depolymerizing at its pole and thus elongate.
source: Similarly, locally pulling on a k-fiber with a microneedle causes it to stop depolymerizing at its pole and thus elongate (Long et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Long et al., 2020.

claim: Inhibiting dynein unfocuses poles but spindles still form albeit with altered lengths in Drosophila and Xenopus.
source: Similarly, inhibiting dynein unfocuses poles but spindles still form albeit with altered lengths in Drosophila (Goshima et al., 2005b) and Xenopus (Gaetz and Kapoor, 2004; Heald et al., 1996; Merdes et al., 1996), and without a clear effect on mammalian spindle length (Guild et al., 2017; Howell et al., 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work (Goshima et al., 2005b; Gaetz and Kapoor, 2004; Heald et al., 1996; Merdes et al., 1996; Guild et al., 2017; Howell et al., 2001).

claim: It is possible to alter kinetochores and microtubule dynamics to shorten k-fibers without a corresponding decrease in the spindle's apparent length.
source: Further, it is possible to alter kinetochores and microtubule dynamics to shorten k-fibers without a corresponding decrease in the spindle's apparent length (DeLuca et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to DeLuca et al., 2006.

claim: Mammalian spindles can achieve similar architecture whether or not dynein (or its recruiter NuMA) is knocked out.
source: However, recent work has revealed that mammalian spindles can achieve similar architecture whether or not dynein (or its recruiter NuMA) is knocked out (Neahring et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Neahring et al., 2021.

claim: The severe defects in spindle coordination and maintenance observed in p50-unfocused spindles are more likely due to the loss of spindle poles than due to the loss of dynein activity per se.
source: This suggests that the severe defects in spindle coordination (Figures 1 and 5) and maintenance (Figure 2) observed in p50-unfocused spindles are more likely due to the loss of spindle poles than due to the loss of dynein activity per se.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that dynein knockout does not produce similar defects as p50 overexpression.

claim: Centrosomes are disconnected from the spindle in unfocused spindles.
source: Additionally, centrosomes are disconnected from the spindle (Figure 1—videos 2 and 3), ruling out contributions from centrosomes (Khodjakov et al., 2000) or astral microtubules on k-fiber length regulation at metaphase.
evidence: The claim is supported by observations shown in Figure 1—videos 2 and 3, and a citation to Khodjakov et al., 2000.

claim: Mammalian spindle poles are required for spindle positioning.
source: Mammalian spindle poles are also required for spindle positioning (Kiyomitsu and Cheeseman, 2012) and have been proposed to help segregate centrosomes (Friedländer and Wahrman, 1970).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Kiyomitsu and Cheeseman, 2012 and Friedländer and Wahrman, 1970.

claim: While k-fibers establish their mean lengths locally, global cues homogenize them.
source: For example, we have shown that while k-fibers establish their mean lengths locally, global cues homogenize them (Figure 1E, G).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1E and G.

claim: The structural integrity and flexible remodeling of other higher-order structures may also rely on individual parts having all the necessary intrinsic information and self-organization to get the correct linear architecture, with global cues organizing these parts in space and time.
source: We put forward the idea that the structural integrity and flexible remodeling of other higher-order structures may also rely on individual parts having all the necessary intrinsic information and self-organization to get the correct linear architecture, with global cues organizing these parts in space and time.
evidence: The claim is a speculative proposal based on the findings of the study.
